why: Idiomatic British reportage - the kind of long-form trade piece ELF actually draws on. The technical register ('scope', 'sinker', 'swivel', 'a floating aid is fixed to nothing; it is moored') is used the way a practitioner would use it, and each term is glossed in passing rather than explained at the reader.
The opening and closing frame (buoy 43 lifted at twenty past six, back over the side by nine, deck hosed down) does real work: it makes the argument in the middle feel observed rather than assembled.

q2 is the best item in the unit. It asks for the mechanism, not the fact, and B is the same idea with the sign reversed - more chain means a wider circle, not a tighter one. A reader who half-understood scope will pick B.

q3 could look like it has two readings: A (marked positions were already uncertain before loggers) and D (the old keepers watched their position more closely than today's crews). D falls away because the text never sets the keepers against present-day crews - it uses them to date the uncertainty, and Fewtrell's quote ('We knew the shoal was under us. Where we were over it was another question') is about the problem, not about diligence. I settled on A without lasting doubt, but D is the closest call in the six units.
q4 rewards reading the concession precisely: Cadell moved on the inshore aids and not on the outer stations. A ('given it up') and C (causal story about the storm) are both clean overreaches.

The penultimate paragraph is unusually honest for a synthetic passage - it says outright that neither record settles the question (two losses in ten years is too thin a series, no grounding traced to the wander). That is what makes q5's B, with its 'unsettled argument', the only defensible main-idea option.

Technically sound in a way that survives checking: the five partials named (hum, prime, minor third, fifth, nominal an octave above the prime) are the standard true-harmonic stack, tuning by removing metal from the inner wall is how it is really done, and 'nothing pulls it back up' is the correct one-way constraint. Nothing here reads as invented.

The economics are stated crisply and then used - bronze billed by the kilo, tuning by the hour, and lathe time not scaling with weight. q1 tests exactly that asymmetry, and C is the intuitive-but-wrong scaling assumption a reader will bring in from outside.

q3 is a properly inferential item. The text never says 'a founder who tunes all five tightly must cast heavier'; the reader has to join the casting allowance, the one-way arrow, and the 'four kilos apart at the pour' in the final paragraph. Satisfying to solve and hard to guess.
Arithmetic reconciles: 240 kg off the mould, 228 kg finished, 12 kg of allowance.

q4 is fair because the writer's restraint is genuinely on the page - Voregg is given the line that limits the Ockthorne trial ('One afternoon, one tower, bells of different weights'), and the writer separately notes that the decisive two-bell experiment has never been paid for. B is ruled out precisely by that sentence: the question is not called unsettleable, only unfunded.
'You can hear a bell that has been argued with' is a strong line and does not feel machine-made.

Reads as a real local-government science story, and the underlying ecology is right: thermal range inside a roof void, bats shifting through a gradient rather than selecting one temperature, woodcrete boxes buffering too well, autumn-to-February installation. A reader with any background knowledge is rewarded, not tripped.

The argument is unusually well-built for a five-question unit. Oyelaran's timing objection is granted outright ('On the early boxes she was plainly right, and Talbourne says so'), and Talbourne answers it not by rebutting but by holding timing constant in a second series. That is the structure the whole unit turns on and it is legible on one read.

The trial numbers close without leftovers: 24 boxes, 12 timber (9 occupied, 3 empty, one of those under an all-night-lit yard) and 12 cast (2 used, both on a warm chimney breast, others on south-facing walls empty). I checked because q3 depends on it, and it holds.
q3 is the sharpest item - the two occupied cast boxes look like evidence for cast boxes until the flue sentence turns them into evidence for the swing. C is the trap and it is a good one.

q4 needs the reader to hold a two-part verdict at once (she is right about the early boxes, and her objection does not reach the second series). The options are written as attitude labels plus a gloss, which made the discrimination easy once I had the structure; A and D are both too blunt to survive the text.

Talbourne's untested suspicion about the lit yard, the fire officer's query on the timber clause, and the fact that nothing reaches the boxes already on walls are all left open. They read as authentic institutional loose ends and none of them is needed to answer anything.

Reads as an authentic Swedish popular-history feature: the vocabulary (stybb, förkolna, stig, tjärdal, hygge, sockenstämmoprotokoll) is period-correct and used without strain, and the researcher-vs-critic structure (Bostrand / Nyfeldt / Bostrand's partial concession) is a shape HP LAS uses often.

The passage is long and entity-dense (Grubbfors, Vresfallet, Slädbo, Bräntemåla, Stråkåsen, plus two named scholars). I had to re-scan to keep the place names apart, but nothing in the questions depends on telling them apart, so it cost time rather than comprehension.

q1: D is a well-built trap - it is the same causal story as B but with 'ofelbart … oavsett hur snabbt kolaren hinner ingripa' bolted on, which the text's 'fick sitta kvar obemärkt' explicitly excludes. Good discrimination.

q2: B is real-world plausible (bulk vs. value-density) but is simply not the reason the text gives; a reader who reasons from general knowledge instead of the third paragraph will land there. That is a legitimate HP trap, not a flaw.

q4: the inference is properly two-step - the 'Årstiderna skilde dem åt' sentence plus the 'ungefär en tredjedel levererade också tjära' sentence. B is excluded by the fraction and A by the explicit statement that the two crafts demanded different skills, so only C survives.

Several details carry no question load (the 1868 debit that stands unexplained for twelve years, the kolardotter who could hear a mila going wrong, the forest administration's complaints). They read as authentic texture rather than as padding, which is how real HP passages behave.

The strongest of the three Swedish units for voice. It is a book review and it sounds like one throughout - the measured praise ('som handbok är den utmärkt'), the reservation introduced as a wish ('den fråga jag helst hade sett mer om'), and the closing utility verdict. Register is consistent from first line to last.
The metaphor work ('en bank vars valuta var säd', 'räntan togs i det enda som fanns i överflöd de goda åren') is the kind of writing HP actually reprints. No calque smell.

q2 is the cleanest item in the set: three of the four options are each contradicted by a specific clause of the 1798 ordinance (two keys held by two people, same-day entry, föreståndare chosen by the sockenstämma), so the distractors are all disprovable rather than merely unattractive.

q3: C is a good near-miss - it is the right target (the sparbank explanation) pushed one notch too far by 'ingen enda av socknarna', which the paragraph about three matching parishes rules out. I had to read that paragraph twice, which is the correct amount of work.

q4 turns on the reviewer's 'Det är det inte' rebuttal of Grimlund's own framing. C inverts who is doing the dwelling - the reviewer wants twenty more pages, Grimlund passes over it - so the item rewards tracking whose judgement is whose.

q1's key is close to a verbatim lift of the second paragraph's second sentence. That makes it an easy opener, which suits position 1, but it is the one item in this unit a test-wise reader could match by string rather than by understanding.

Convincing as a Swedish technology-history feature. The physical detail is coherent and self-consistent rather than decorative: the square-cube argument ('fördubblas kantlängden blir ytan fyra gånger så stor och volymen åtta') is stated correctly and then actually used to justify Lorentzon's rule, so the passage rewards a reader who follows the reasoning.
Old units reconcile: two fot given as 'knappt sextio centimeter' and four alnar as 'knappt två och en halv meter' both match the Swedish values. A reader who checks is not punished.

q2 requires separating Karnstedt's objection (the reconstruction is tighter than the old houses, so it says little about spånlagret in them) from Frodell's own claim (packing did the work). B hands back Frodell's position as if it were the objection - a genuine attention test, and a fair one.

q3 is my favourite item here: the fish dealer's cupboard looks like a counterexample to the whole article until the sentence 'de var inga misstag' reframes it as an economic calculation. C is exactly the reading a hurried reader will take.
q4's date arithmetic (rule written 1901, reconstruction 2011) supports 'mer än hundra år senare' without being stated, which is a nice light inference for the closing item.

The Mörtsjön paragraph deliberately closes off without resolution ('någon jämförande stapel … har aldrig kommit till stånd'). It carries no question, and I briefly expected one from it, but it reads as authentic honesty about an open question rather than as a dangling thread.
